idiom_name: enum match arms over syn::Expr (visit/visit-mut/fold traits) - the rule table is the match
implementation_notes: Rust's own pattern matching is the matcher: an enum tree is destructured with match arms, refutable patterns, guards and bindings, and the traversal comes from syn's visit, visit-mut or fold traits - each has a default method per node type that recurses - or from a small recursive function you write. A rewrite is fold_expr returning a replacement Expr, which is exactly pattern plus action with the trait default owning the walk; syn needs the visit, visit-mut or fold feature, and quote! plus parse_quote! build the replacement. Because match arms are exhaustiveness-checked, an unhandled node variant is a compile error rather than a silent non-match, which is the main advantage over a rule bag; macro_rules token-tree matching and the compiler's HIR are different mechanisms for different trees.
pitfalls: fold takes and rebuilds owned nodes, so returning a fresh node for every input loses identity and allocates; return the original when nothing matched to keep the rewrite local.
Matching through owning wrappers is awkward: patterns on Box<Expr> move the value, so a rule that needs both a subtree and its children must restructure the match (or clone) instead of binding twice.

syn parses with its own feature set and treats macro bodies as token streams, so a rule over syn::File silently cannot see inside macro invocations - a different tree (rustc HIR, or token matching) is needed there.
